_source.displaydescription:
The Umāmaheśvara temple is located in Cāka Bāhāḥ Ṭola and stands on a three-tier plinth. It has a composite roof type which combines a tiered roof and a dome. Before 1934 earthquake, the temple had three tiers and was constructed in the style of a pagoda. However, it was levelled by the earthquake and reconstructed in this mixed style. This temple is located approximately 8 m east of the Nārāyaṇa Temple (LAL2740), and together they form a complex with streets passing by to the west and south. Residential houses surround the square, which has now almost turned into a market place; street vendors occupy most of the open space.

The sanctum of the temple can be accessed via stone steps to the west. Two stone lions sit on the first plinth level to guard the deities inside. At the southwest corner of the plinth, one can find a hanging bell that was donated in 2012. A statue of Nandī (vehicle of Śiva) is in front of the temple, and a trident has been erected close to this icon. The entrance to the sanctum is clad in metal, and has a toraṇa with an image of Garuḍa on top and Umā-Maheśvara at the centre, flanked by Gaṇeśa and Kumāra. The roofs as well as the columns are clad in copper. On top of the roof, one can see a pinnacle alongside a metal trident. A serpent covers the top of the pinnacle, while four other snakes creep up to the tip of the second roof from each of the bottom four corners.

The main sanctum is a square room with doorways on all four sides. Inside, one can find a four-faced śivaliṅga clad in brass. Of the four doors, the western door is the main entry way. Surmounted by a torana, the entryway is encased in carved metal sheets and has a raised stone threshold (29 cm), while the other doors are much more simple and plain. A stone statue of Umāmaheśvara is attached to the eastern wall, and the sanctum also contains images of Śrīdevī, Bhūdevī, Viṣṇu and Sūrya (sitting on a chariot pulled by seven horses). The image of Sūrya (the Sun god) is a recreation of the archaic one, which was stolen some decades ago. Pruscha (1975, 209) mentions that there was once an image of Candramā (the Moon god) here, though there is no other proof of this.

The stone inscription attached above the southern door of the temple mentions that the monument was reconstructed by Viśvambhara Bhāro in NS 796 (CE 1676) during the reign of King Śrīnivāsa Malla. The inscription further informs readers that the King and his son Yoganarendra Malla were also present at the consecration of the temple, where lands were bestowed and a guṭhī was established to fund its ritual worship However, these days no guṭhī lands connected to the temple could be traced. In VS 2058, local people collected donations in order to try to continue the daily and other ritual worships of the temple. They assigned a Brahmin from Agniśālā Ṭola to carry out this task. However, the earthquake 2015 further hindered the daily worship. The Cakravarti Ṭola Sudhāra Samiti (an organisation for local development) is currently responsible for opening and closing the temple.

_source.displaydescription:
The caitya is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) and is part of a group of four caityas and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala which are alligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the caitya is paved with black flagstone and has been encroached upon by building materials for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira.

Generally, caityas follow a pattern of placing statues of Akṣobhya to the east, Amoghasiddhi to the north, Amitābha to the west and Ratnasambhava to the south. However, this caitya has Vairocana facing east, Mañjuśrī north, Vajrasattva west and Amitābha south.

The caitya was built in 1962. A special worship was organised in the courtyard for the welfare of the community three months before its construction began. During the worship, donations were collected to fund its construction. On the full moon day of Āśvina an umbrella is placed on top of the caitya and on the full moon day of Vaiśākhaits the anniversary worship is performed.

Iku Bāhāḥ, a very small, private bāhāḥ, is located in Ikhālakhu Ṭola, about 35m northeast of the Ikhālakhu square. Since there is no entrance through any of the streets, one must enter through the door of a private building situated towards the west of the monument. 

At the centre of the courtyard, there is a small shrine facing east with just a small opening that is 55cm wide and raised on a one meter-high platform. Inside the shrine is a tiny image of Akṣobhya Buddha. One might notice the unusual proportions of the statue of the Buddha and the large lotus on which he is sitting. A small caitya, made from stone and with images of Tathāgatas facing in all four cardinal directions, forms the pinnacle of the shrine. In front of the shrine, there is a dharmadhātu caitya in octagonal shape. There are images of eight Lokeśvaras on the dharmadhātu: Vajrapāṇi, Gaganagañja, Ratnapāṇi, Kṣitigarbha, Padmapāṇi, Viśvapāṇi, Ratnagarbha and Sarvanivaraṇaviṣkambhin.

On the northern wall of the residential building, one can find a niche containing an aniconic stone statue that is worshiped as Gaṇeśa. At the west wall of the āgãchẽ is a khaḍga. The āgãchẽ of the Bāhāḥ is to the northernmost end of the courtyard, and it is possible to exit via the northeastern corner.

Pruscha writes, “all that has remained of this Bahal is a small courtyard with plastered shrine and dharmadhatu in the form of a double petalled lotus. The shrine contains an image of Bhumisparsa Shakyamuni. It was constructed by Bekharatna Silakar in 1934 and its chief priest is a Bajracharya.” (Pruscha 2015: 207)

The illustration identified as Ikhālākhu Bāhāḥ on p. 141 in Locke 1985 is actually Iku Bāhāḥ, and the photograph of Ikhālākhu (mislabeled as Iku Bāhāḥ) is in fact on p. 139.

This Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala is located to the west of Karuṇāmaya Mandira (BUN0001) and is part of a group of four caityas, all of which are aligned in a north-south direction. The area surrounding the Dharmadhātu Maṇḍala is paved with black flagstones and has been encroached upon by some of the building materials used for the reconstruction of the Karuṇāmaya Mandira.

The Maṇḍala was constructed in 1964. The inscription does not mention the name of its founder, though locals state that his name was Harṣamuni Śākya.

Bhīmarāja Bāhāḥ is a branch of the Oku Bāhāḥ (LAL2260). It can be accessed via the entrance of a private building that is located at the southwest corner of the Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ (LAL2350). Bhīmarāja Śākya, a member of the saṅgha of Oku Bāhāḥ, established this bāhāḥ.

The structure of the Bhīmarāja Bāhāḥ differs from other bāhāḥ of Patan. This bāhāḥ has no no esoteric god house, and its courtyard  (5.2 m x 5.2 m) contans an uncommon caitya. Located at the very center of the courtyard, this caitya is the main monument of the bāhāḥ and has a structure that is not often seen in the Valley. Four stone pillars have been erected at each of the four corners above its double-layered lotus petals (which together are 96cm in diameter), supporting a layer of stone that forms a roof. A statue of Avalokiteśvara stands on top of the lotus petals, and a stūpa-shaped finial has been placed on the roof. Śākya (1994, 35) calls it a Kūṭāgārākṛti Caitya. It is based on a square plinth measuring 185cm in width and 13cm in height. 

The sanctum has iron railings fixed on three sides, with the western face left free. A small, west-facing marble image of Avalokiteśvara stands inside the sanctum. Adorned in a crown, a large necklace, and a dhoti, the deity is performing varada with his right hand and holding the stem of a lotus in his left.

The courtyard is paved in telia tiles and a plinth surrounds the residential buildings. The three-storey building on the northern side has a colonnaded three-bay phalcā underneath it.

No inscription or any other document could be found to confirm the consecration date of this bāhāḥ. However, Bhīmarāja, the elder brother of Bhājudhana, established the bāhāḥ just after his younger brother established the Bhājudhana Bāhāḥ in 1909 (Śākya 1994, 120).

Nowadays, some small cracks can be seen in the caitya. These were caused by the 2015 earthquake.

Some aniconic stones images worshipped as Lukumāhādyaḥ have been placed at the northeastern corner of the courtyard. Śākya (1994, 121) mentions that a school named Mahābauddha Pāṭhaśālā once operated in this vihāra, and had 150 students. He also writes that there were wall paintings of Vīṇārāja, Khaḍgarāja, Dhvajarāja and Caityarāja on the wall of a house located to the south of the courtyard.
_source.displayname: Bhīmarāja Bāhāḥ (1909 CE) || भीमराज बाहाः ॥ LAL2360

Devajyoti Bāhāḥ is a branch of Bu Bāhāḥ (LAL0440). It is located to the north of Bu Bāhāḥ and can be accessed via a narrow alley that leads from the monument's north-west corner. The main shrine building faces north and stands on a double plinth. It is attached to the rear boundary wall, which is decorated with a pair of pilaster columns on either side. The monument appears to have been constructed relatively recently and has an overhanging concrete roof with a bell-shaped pinnacle and a stūpa above it. The shrine is plastered in lime and has been painted white. A stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined in the sanctum. Small statues of Gaṇeśa and Mahākāla have been attached to the boundary wall, on the left and right-hand sides of the shrine respectively.

The courtyard (6.7 m x 4.2 m) is also home to a dharmadhātujinālaya caitya (180 cm high) and a dharmadhātu maṇḍala (90 cm high), both of which stand in front of the main monument and are lined up in its axis. The courtyard is surrounded by residential buildings and has a colonnaded structure on the ground floor. Two bells hang from the stone pillars on the eastern and western sides of the courtyard.

This bāhāḥ was established by Devajyoti Vajrācārya in 1889. After his death, his wives established a guṭhī for the management of the bāhāḥ in 1897. The Mūladuvā clan (a priest clan) of Bu Bāhāḥ performs the daily worship in this shrine. Aside from this, all other social and religious activities related to this bāhāḥ have come to an end.
_source.displayname: Devajyoti Bāhāḥ (1889 CE) || देवज्योति बाहा: || LAL0451

Local residents still remember the open water channel [deydhaḥ (desadhala)] that used to run through Sunāguthi. A small pit (kuṇḍa) called Capĩgāḥ is located on the bank of this water channel and was once used to collect water. This water was considered to be holy and was offered to the statue of Bālakūmāri located in the temple to the east (SUN0230). A local religious song also mentions bathing in the Capĩgāḥ. The royal water channel (rājakulo) dates back to the 9th century and used to supply water from Lele to Patan and the villages along its route. A road widening project undertaken in 2012 necessisted the closing of the formerly open water channel and the water was diverted into underground cement pipes. The Capĩgāḥ was filled with rubble, and the current water tank made of brick and cement was constructed in its place. This tank remains empty and appears to be neglected. According to local informants, the tank is filled with water only once a year, on the full moon day of Caitra during the celebration of a jātrā. When the procession cots stop in front of the Bālakūmāri Temple, water from the Capĩgāḥ is sprinkled on the cots.

This Capĩgāḥ stands as an example of tangible and intangible heritage that has been severely affected by modern construction work.

Dune Bāhāḥ, a branch of Si Bāhāḥ (LAL0690), is located to the west of the main Bāhāḥ and faces towards it also. Tall buildings surround the courtyard in which the building is located. The Bāhāḥ is also known as Bāhāḥcā, though its classical name is Duṇḍagṛha Bāhāḥ. Pruscha (1975, P-70) calls it Kaccā Bāhāḥ and Locke (1985, 174) mentions it as Bāchā Bāhāḥ.  

The ground floor sanctum is paved with stones and can be reached through a central door flanked by the statue of Gaṇeśa to the left and Mahākāla to the right. A stone statue of Prajñāpāramitā is attached to the wall above the entrance of the sanctum, and a stone statue of Akṣobhya is enshrined in the sanctum. The Bāhāḥ's carved door frames are its original ones, though the door leaves have been replaced with more simple framed metal shutters. The façade of the two-storey building is completely covered with cement plaster and a simple band of cornice marks the separate floors. Three small cement lattice windows have been placed asymmetrically on the first floor. Four plain struts support the overhanging corrugated metal sheet roof. Most of the original architecture of the building can no longer be found in this structure.

A śikharakūṭa caitya (130 cm high) is located at the centre of the courtyard, the base of which is covered by the raised stone flooring. 

No historical record with which one could date Bāhāḥ could be made available. Pruscha (P-70) suggests that it was built some time around the 17th century. In 1971, the Bāhāḥ was renovated and this was funded by selling a piece of its land. Śākyas are the saṅgha members of the Bāhāḥ; two families perform its daily ritual worships. The responsibility for this is passed on between families every 15 days.

Three small cement lattice windows have been placed asymmetrically on the first floor. Four plain struts support the overhanging corrugated metal sheet roof. Most of the original architecture of the building can no longer be found in this structure.

A śikharakūṭa caitya (130 cm high) is located at the centre of the courtyard, the base of which is covered by the raised stone flooring. 

No historical record with which one could date Bāhāḥ could be made available. Pruscha (P-70) suggests that it was built some time around the 17th century. In 1971, the Bāhāḥ was renovated and this was funded by selling a piece of its land. Śākyas are the saṅgha members of the Bāhāḥ; two families perform its daily ritual worships. The responsibility for this is passed on between families every 15 days.
